unit.title: Classifying Living Things
unit.blurb: How to tell if something is alive, whether viruses are living, why and how scientists sort organisms into groups, and how to use and build keys.

O1.t: Describe the seven characteristics of living organisms (MRS GREN).

O2.t: Discuss reasons why viruses can be thought of as living or non-living.

O3.t: Understand that a species is a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.

O4.t: Explain why scientists classify living things, how classification has developed and how scientific names work.

O5.t: Classify plants and animals into their main groups using observable features.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 4: Classifying Living Things.
We will learn how to tell if something is alive,
whether viruses are living, why scientists sort organisms into groups,
and how to use keys to identify them.
Indonesia is home to around 50,000 species of plants and animals,
including 515 kinds of mammals, more than any other country,
and over 1500 kinds of birds.
We say it has a rich biodiversity.
With so many living things, scientists sort them into groups.
This is called classification.
It makes them easier to study,
and it helps us protect endangered animals like the Sumatran tiger.
How can we tell if something is alive?
All living things, or organisms, are made of cells,
and they all carry out seven life processes.
A plant is living, but the pot it grows in is not.
Remember them with the name MRS GREN.
M is for movement, and R is for respiration.
S is for sensitivity, and G is for growth.
R is for reproduction, and E is for excretion.
And N is for nutrition.
Every living thing does all seven!
All living things show movement.
Animals move from place to place: birds fly and frogs hop.
Plants move too, but slowly.
Climbing plants wind around objects, and some flowers turn to follow the Sun.
Nutrition is how living things get food.
Plants and algae make their own food by photosynthesis, using the Sun's energy,
carbon dioxide and water.
Animals cannot make their own food.
They feed on plants, animals and other living things,
like this chameleon catching an insect.
Living things grow. A tadpole grows into an adult frog,
and a tulip bulb grows into a plant.
Organisms get bigger when the number of their cells increases,
or when their cells get bigger.
Growth needs food and energy.
Mix yeast, sugar and water, and after an hour you see bubbles.
The yeast is alive: it respires and releases a waste gas.
Respiration is a series of chemical reactions in cells that releases energy from food.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and takes place in the mitochondria.
Yeast is a fungus used to make bread.
Bottle A has yeast, warm water and sugar.
Bottle B has yeast and warm water but no sugar.
A balloon is stretched over each bottle.
Predict: what will happen to the balloons after one hour?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Both bottles are kept warm, at thirty-five degrees Celsius, for one hour.
Bottle A is full of bubbles, and its balloon has blown up.
The balloon on bottle B has hardly changed.
Explain what you saw.
The yeast in bottle A used the sugar as food and respired.
Respiration released carbon dioxide gas, which blew up the balloon.
Without sugar, the yeast in bottle B had no food.
So yeast shows nutrition and respiration: it is alive.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
All living things can sense changes in their environment and respond to them.
This is called sensitivity.
Earthworms move away from light.
Fish have special cells along their sides that sense movements in the water,
warning them of predators.
And we sweat when we get hot.
Plants are sensitive too.
The sundew's sticky leaves close over insects that land on them,
and the evening primrose opens its flowers as the Sun sets,
to attract moths.
Reproduction means producing offspring.
Lions give birth to live young, ostrich chicks hatch from eggs,
and plants make new plants from seeds, spores, roots or leaves.
Chemical reactions in cells make waste products,
which would harm the organism if they built up.
Excretion removes them. Plants release waste gases through tiny holes in their leaves called stomata.
Humans excrete carbon dioxide through the lungs.
The kidneys make urine, containing water, urea and salts.
And our skin releases water, salts and a little urea when we sweat.

captions: What makes us catch a cold or chickenpox?
Often, a virus. Viruses are much smaller than bacteria;
we need very powerful microscopes to see them.
A virus particle is just genetic material, such as DNA,
wrapped in a protein coat.
Some also have an outer envelope.
Different viruses attack plants, bacteria or animals.
A virus copies itself by invading a living cell, called a host cell,
and releasing its genetic material inside.
The virus uses the host cell to make many copies of itself.
The new viruses burst out, often destroying the cell,
and go on to infect other cells.
So, are viruses alive?
Scientists are still debating this question!
Let's test them against the characteristics of living things.
Viruses are not made of cells.
They have no mitochondria, so they don't respire.
They don't feed or excrete, and they can't move by themselves;
they are carried by air or liquids, like when you sneeze.
But viruses do have genetic material,
and they can make copies of themselves inside a suitable host cell.
Those are features of living things.
So virus particles are usually thought of as non-living.
But some scientists say that inside a host cell,
the virus and the cell together form a living unit.
Viruses affect people, animals and plants every day.
Here are four real examples.
Most colds are caused by rhinoviruses.
They invade the cells lining your nose and throat,
and make copies of themselves.
Vaccines train the body to recognise a virus, such as the measles virus,
before it can make us ill.
Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they do not work against viruses.
Taking them for a cold does not help.
Plants catch viruses too.
The tobacco mosaic virus makes patchy, mottled leaves on tomato and pepper plants.
Pause and decide: why does a doctor not give antibiotics for a cold?

captions: Scientists have named about 1.5 million kinds of living things so far,
but they think there may be 30 to 50 million on Earth!
Biodiversity measures how many different kinds of living things, or species,
live in an area.
The more species, the more biodiverse it is.
In Singapore, forests have been cleared since 1819 for farms, buildings and roads.
A 2023 study found Singapore has lost about 37 percent of its biodiversity,
and only 1 percent of the original forest remains.
Now nature reserves protect the remaining forest, and the oriental pied hornbill,
once lost from Singapore, has returned.
Scientists have named and classified about one and a half million species so far.
This bar chart shows roughly how many are known in some groups,
in thousands.
Insects are by far the largest group: about one million named species.
There are about three hundred and ninety thousand plants,
and about six and a half thousand mammals.
Many more species are still waiting to be found, especially insects in rainforests.
Pause and use the chart:
roughly how many times more named insect species are there than plant species?
Classification means sorting and grouping things according to their similarities,
just like books in a library.
Classifying living things helps us to identify and name them,
study them more easily, understand how they are related,
and communicate accurately about them.
The most useful characteristics include body shape and skeleton,
body parts like feathers or legs, the life cycle and how they reproduce,
and their genetic makeup.
Some features are not useful.
A ladybird and a frog can both have spots,
but they are not closely related at all!
Around 2400 years ago, Aristotle divided living things into just two groups: plants,
which are green and don't move, and animals, which move.
In the 1700s, the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus grouped organisms by
their observed features and invented the two-word scientific naming system.
Microscopes revealed much more.
In the 1960s, R.
H. Whittaker sorted living things into five kingdoms, based on cell structure, cell walls,
reproduction and nutrition.
Later, genetic studies showed that the Monera were really two different groups.
So today most scientists use six kingdoms.
Scientific knowledge keeps developing!
Kingdoms are divided into smaller and smaller groups.
Let's classify a human.
Humans are in the animal kingdom,
the chordate phylum of animals with a backbone, and the mammal class.
Then the primate order, the hominid family and the genus Homo.
The smallest group is the species: Homo sapiens, which means wise man.
Today scientists can also identify a species from its DNA.
A section of DNA is analysed to give a pattern of bands,
like a barcode. Comparing barcodes shows how species are related.
So what exactly is a species?
It is a group of organisms that can reproduce with
one another to produce offspring that can also reproduce.
We call these offspring fertile.
A rooster and a hen are the same species.
Their chicks grow up and can have chicks of their own.
Very rarely, two different species breed.
A yak and a cow can produce a dzo,
a hybrid used as a pack animal in the Himalayas.
But hybrids like this are usually infertile: they cannot produce offspring.
Common names can be confusing.
The robin in America is a totally different bird from the robin in Europe!
So every known species has a scientific name with two parts in Latin,
written in italics. The first word is the genus, with a capital letter.
The second is the species, in lower case.
Humans are Homo sapiens.
Scientific names show relationships.
The leopard and the snow leopard are both in the genus Panthera,
so they are closely related.
Each scientific name is unique,
so scientists around the world know exactly which organism they mean,
for example the bacterium that causes tuberculosis.
chapters: Real data: named species in some groups

req.prompt: What is a species?

captions: Plants can be classified using their characteristics,
such as whether they form seeds or flowers.
Some plants do not form seeds, like mosses and ferns.
Ferns reproduce from spores.
Other plants do form seeds.
Seed plants are either flowering plants, with seeds inside fruits, or conifers,
non-flowering plants with seeds in cones, like a pine tree.
Animals are divided into two main groups.
Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.
Arthropods have jointed legs.
Insects have three body sections and six legs, while arachnids, like spiders,
have two body sections and eight legs.
Molluscs, like snails, have no jointed legs.
Vertebrates are animals with a backbone.
There are five groups of vertebrates: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Some animals are easy to classify, but others can trick us.
Predict which of these four are vertebrates before each answer appears.
A bat flies like a bird, but it is a mammal.
It has a backbone, fur, and feeds its young on milk.
Vertebrate.
A starfish lives in the sea but it is not a fish.
It has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate.
A seahorse looks strange, but it is a real fish, with a backbone,
gills and fins. Vertebrate.
A spider has eight jointed legs and two body sections.
It is an arachnid, an invertebrate.
So classify an animal by its features,
not by where it lives or how it moves.
Pause and classify a whale: which vertebrate group is it in?
Sadly, human activities have made many vertebrates endangered, or even extinct.
Great hammerhead sharks are endangered by overfishing for their fins.
Axolotls are endangered because their wetland homes were drained for farms and buildings.
The Round Island burrowing boa was last seen in 1975,
after people brought cats and rats to its island.
The great auk was hunted to extinction by 1844.
And in 2019, the Bramble Cay melomys became extinct after rising seas and storms,
caused by climate change, flooded its island home.

captions: How can we identify a living thing we don't recognise?
We use a dichotomous key.
Dichotomous means dividing into two.
At each step there are two choices.
Start at the top.
Does the insect have wings?
If yes, does it have a protective cover over its wings?
If it does, a rounded body means a ladybird, and a long,
flat body means a cockroach.
Wings with no protective cover?
It's a moth.
No wings at all?
Very long antennae means a silverfish; short antennae means a flea.
Follow the branches until you reach a name!
A key can also be a list of paired statements.
Let's identify this mystery plant, which has seeds but no flowers.
Step 1: the plant has cones, so choose 1a and go to 2.
Step 2: the cones are large, so choose 2a and go to 3.
Step 3: the leaves are narrow, so choose 3b and go to 4.
Step 4: the leaves are fern-like, so choose 4b.
The plant is a cycad!
Now try making your own dichotomous key, for example for six different mammals.
First, observe the characteristics of all the organisms carefully.
Then choose a feature that divides them into two groups: some have it,
and some don't. For example: has legs, or does not have legs.
Look at each smaller group and choose another feature to divide it again.
Repeat until every organism has its own name at the end of a branch.
Use visible features that don't vary, like the number of legs,
and test your key by swapping it with a classmate!
Here are four animals: an eagle, a shark, a frog and a bee.
We want a key with yes or no questions.
Predict: which first question would split them into two groups?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The first question is: does it have a backbone?
Only the bee has no backbone, so the bee is identified.
Next: does it have feathers?
Only the eagle has feathers.
Last: does it have gills and fins?
Yes for the shark, no for the frog.
Every animal now has its own branch.
Explain why these questions work.
Each one asks about a clear feature that
we can see and that does not change,
so it splits the group into two.
A question like is it big, or is it pretty, would not work,
because people would answer differently.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
